# Steam Turbines
# Operation
The Standard boiler burns fuel from a removable Standard hopper or tank. It needs room oxygen and a water-filled internal reservoir. Fuel heat raises steam temperature and pressure; pressure limits electrical output while the turbine warms up or loses water. The turbine has a slow electrical ramp, so pair it with stored power for sudden loads.
Stop the machine and open its maintenance panel to install or remove a fuel module. Close the panel to add fuel or pour pure water into the reservoir. Examine the water, pressure and temperature gauges. The internal condenser returns most water; a little escapes as hot water vapor. Burning fuel also releases carbon dioxide into the room.
The basic 250u reservoir lasts about four hours at rated output. The water gauge reaches its low range near 10 percent; falling pressure throttles power and eventually trips the turbine. Refill and restart it manually. A basic 1500u tank of Welding Fuel lasts about two and a half hours at rated output. Wood, coal, plasma and fuel-grade plasma use the same Standard hopper as the Stirling generator. Weaker fuels require more stoking to hold boiler temperature.
Its efficient rating is 40 kW. The basic target ceiling is 60 kW; better capacitors can raise it to 72 kW. Higher targets need hotter steam and greater pressure, and above 40 kW fuel consumption grows faster than electrical output. Extra burning also releases more carbon dioxide and hot water vapor. The hotter boiler increases rupture risk.
# Commercial
Commercial uses its own larger removable hopper or tank and blocks sight across its 2×3 footprint. It supplies 60 kW efficiently, with a 90 kW basic ceiling and 108 kW ceiling with R4 capacitors. Its base ramp is 3 kW/s. A 2250u Welding Fuel tank lasts about three hours at rating; the manually filled 500u water reservoir lasts about five hours. Higher targets increase consumption and emissions.
Connect either or both red exhaust ports on the north edge. Either or both blue intake ports on the south edge can draw piped air. The ports rotate with the machine and use only the primary pipe layer; use manifolds to connect other layers. An unconnected intake uses room air; a connected intake needs oxygen in its pipe. Exhaust must be connected to a network that can remove the waste gas. Routine carbon dioxide, unused intake gases and lost steam enter the connected exhaust pipes, while damage leaks and ruptures escape into the room. The least-pressurized connected exhaust controls the throttle. Above 300 kPa it reduces output and fuel burn; at 600 kPa on every outlet, or if all exhausts are disconnected, the machine shuts down and requires a manual restart.
Standard rated steam is 650 K at 3000 kPa above ambient; Commercial is 700 K at 5000 kPa above ambient. The pressure gauge represents the boiler, not the much lower-pressure exhaust pipe. The internal condenser and pressure behavior are simplified.
# Status Indicators
The fuel square is black for a solid hopper or green for a liquid tank. The blue W square shows water level; P shows boiler pressure and T shows temperature. Fuel and water lamps turn red when empty, amber when low, and green as supplies increase. Pressure and temperature lamps are grey while cold or depressurized, amber while rising, green around normal operation, and red in their high range. Examine the gauges for exact readings.
# Damage
At 20 percent chassis damage, the boiler begins venting hot water vapor on damage steps. Further hits vent more water and lower pressure. Damaged seals also lose retained pressure, and rebuilding pressure takes time. Escaping hot steam can scald exposed people near the casing; protective clothing reduces heat transfer. Repairing the chassis restores sealing but does not replace lost water.
A single hit dealing at least 25 percent of maximum chassis durability after resistance can catastrophically rupture a pressurized boiler, even before the chassis would normally be destroyed. Standard needs 25 damage in one hit; Commercial needs 45. Separate small hits do not add together for this trigger. A depressurized boiler cannot produce a pressure blast; a small finishing hit breaks and vents it without the catastrophic explosion.
A pressure rupture damages the machine and its immediate surroundings. Commercial blast damage reaches about 2.25 metres at rated pressure and 3 metres at maximum pressure. Only tiles directly beneath the Commercial chassis can lose plating, and each has a chance to remain intact. Standard blasts preserve plating and reach about 1.5 to 2 metres. The initial flash can look larger than the damaging blast; lingering fires follow actual spilled fuel. Escaped burner fuel can also burn in oxygen. Switching off does not instantly remove pressure: a cooling boiler remains dangerous until its gauge falls. The casing warms the room, including while a stopped boiler cools. Keep ventilation and gas scrubbing available. Standard requires a 2×2 machine frame; Commercial requires a 2×3 frame. A normal machine frame is too small.
